summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for managing demand access circuits, including ISDN, using SMIv2. It lets management tools monitor dial-up calls.

plainLanguage.summary: A log and control panel for lines that only connect when you need them.

questions: what is the dial control mib
what is a demand access circuit
how does the dial control mib store call history
subtitle: An SNMP MIB for peers, active calls and call history on lines that only connect on demand, such as ISDN.

tldr.problem: Dial-up and ISDN links connect only when needed, and a given peer can be reached over different channels at different times, so ordinary per-interface management does not describe who is called, when and why.
tldr.mechanism: The Dial Control MIB defines four groups: general configuration, peer configuration and statistics, active calls, and call history. Each peer gets its own logical interface that is tied to the low-level channels with the ifStack table.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that is generic enough for modems and X.25 virtual connections as well as ISDN, and it is the companion MIB that the ISDN MIB (RFC 2127) requires.

today: RFC 2128 is a Proposed Standard published in March 1997, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The ISDN MIB in RFC 2127 requires it to be implemented alongside.

sections.title: What the Dial Control MIB Is
sections.content:
RFC 2128 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) that describes managed objects for demand access circuits, including ISDN. These are links that are brought up when needed and taken down afterwards. The module is written in SMIv2 and fits the SNMP framework: the SMI (RFC 1902), MIB-II (RFC 1213) and the protocol (RFC 1157 and/or RFC 1905).

It was produced by the ISDN MIB working group of the IETF, and it is the companion of the ISDN MIB in RFC 2127. Splitting the two lets this part be reused for interfaces other than ISDN.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a standard way to describe a connection that is not always on, like a dial-up line, so management tools can read about it.

sections.title: Four Groups of Information
sections.content:
Managing demand access circuits requires general configuration, peer configuration and statistics, active call information and call history. The MIB therefore has four groups.

  • dialCtlConfiguration: general settings.
  • dialCtlPeer: how to connect to each peer on outgoing calls, how to identify peers on incoming calls, and per-peer statistics.
  • callActive: one entry for each call in progress.
  • callHistory: a record of every call, successful, unsuccessful or rejected. An entry is created when a call is cleared.

The history may describe circuit switched calls or virtual circuits.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four notebooks: one for house rules, one with the address book, one listing calls happening right now, and one listing calls that have ended.

sections.title: Peers, Interfaces and Multilink
sections.content:
On a dial-up interface a call to a given peer can float from channel to channel, so you cannot say that a peer is always called on one interface. The MIB solves this by creating a logical interface (ifEntry) for each peer and one for each low-level interface, and relating them with the ifStackTable. Low-level interfaces are either physical, such as modems, or logical, such as ISDN B channels. Each peer must have an encapsulation layer interface of some kind, for example PPP or LAPB.

The Dial Control MIB never creates ifEntry rows itself. An entry in dialCtlPeerCfgTable can only be created if the associated ifEntry already exists, and it has its own RowStatus so the dial control data can come and go without disturbing the ifIndex.

A peer is identified by dialCtlPeerCfgId. Several table entries may share the same id but have different ifIndex values. Each describes a possible connection to the same peer, which supports multilink and backup lines, for example by bundling the interfaces with PPP multilink.
sections.plainLanguage: Each person you might call gets their own name tag. Which phone line is used can change from call to call, and the tag stays the same.

sections.title: Peer Configuration Objects
sections.content:
The general configuration group has two objects. dialCtlAcceptMode sets the security level for incoming calls: acceptNone(1) accepts none, acceptAll(2) accepts even calls with no matching peer entry, and acceptKnown(3) accepts only calls matching an entry in dialCtlPeerCfgTable. dialCtlTrapEnable turns call notifications on for all peers; its default is disabled.

Each row of dialCtlPeerCfgTable holds what is needed to call or recognize a peer: the originate address (the phone number to call), the answer address (the calling party number on incoming calls), a subaddress, a closed user group, the desired speed in bits per second, and the information transfer type (for example speech, unrestrictedDigital, audio31, video or fax). dialCtlPeerCfgPermission says whether the peer may be called, may call, both, callback or none.

Timers control the call: an inactivity timer in seconds (zero means the connection is never taken down for inactivity, so it is a dedicated circuit), minimum and maximum duration, carrier delay, call retries, retry delay and failure delay. The RFC notes that the callback permission is meant to control charging, not security.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address-book entry says who to call, which number to use, what kind of call it is, how long to wait before hanging up, and how many times to retry.

sections.title: Active Calls, History and Notifications
sections.content:
Each row of callActiveTable describes a call in progress: the peer address and id, the interface indexes, setup and connect times, charged units, the call origin and packet and byte counters. callActiveCallState is one of four values, shown below.

When a call clears, an entry goes into callHistoryTable, including the disconnect cause and disconnect time. callHistoryTableMaxLength limits the number of rows; a value of 0 prevents any history from being kept, and when the table is full the oldest entry is deleted. callHistoryRetainTimer, in minutes, sets the minimum time an entry is kept; a value of 0 also prevents history and does not stop completion traps.

Counters such as charged units and packet counts use AbsoluteCounter32, a Counter32-like value that does not decrease or wrap and locks at 4,294,967,295 if it overflows.

Two notifications exist. dialCtlPeerCallInformation is sent when a successful call clears or a failed attempt ultimately fails (after all retries), at most once between successful attempts. dialCtlPeerCallSetup is sent whenever a call setup message is received or sent.
sections.plainLanguage: One notebook shows calls happening right now. When a call ends, a line goes into the history notebook, and the oldest lines are erased when it gets full.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says information in this MIB may be used by upper protocol layers for security purposes. It also warns about generic peers: one way to support them is to allow wild-card characters (a question mark or an asterisk) in dialCtlPeerCfgAnswerAddress. Doing so may create a security hole, because the user would not know where a call is from. That could allow unauthorized access if no other authentication scheme, such as PPP authentication, is available. The specification of generic peers is out of scope for this document.
sections.plainLanguage: If you let anyone call in by using a wildcard phone number, you no longer know who is calling, so you need another way, like a password, to check them.

items.title: dialCtlConfiguration
items.text: General configuration such as the accept mode.

items.title: callHistory
items.text: Records of cleared calls, including failed and rejected ones.

items.desc: An outgoing connection attempt is being made.
